title: John Harrison and the longitude problem

slides.title: The carpenter who saved sailors with a *clock.*
slides.body: How a self-taught craftsman solved the greatest scientific puzzle of his age.

image.credit: John Harrison by Thomas King · Science Museum · Public domain

slides.title: Wrecked off their *own coast*
slides.body: Four Royal Navy warships hit the rocks of the Isles of Scilly. **Between 1,400 and 2,000 sailors die.** Bad charts, faulty compasses, no way to find longitude.

slides.title: Latitude was easy. *Longitude* wasn't.
slides.body: Sailors read latitude from the Sun and stars. Longitude meant knowing the exact time back home, **and no clock could keep time on a rolling ship.**

slides.title: A £20,000 *prize*
slides.body: Parliament passes the Longitude Act: **up to £20,000**, millions today, for a practical way to find longitude at sea. The experts bet on astronomy.

slides.title: A carpenter walks into *London*
slides.body: John Harrison, a self-taught joiner, arrives with H1: a sea clock that **ignores the motion of the ship.** It works on its first trial. He isn't satisfied.

slides.title: Then he makes it *small*
slides.body: After nearly two decades on his third clock, Harrison changes direction. H4 is **a large pocket watch, about 13 cm across.**

image.credit: Harrison's H4 · Photo: Colonel Warden · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

slides.title: 81 days at *sea*
slides.body: H4 sails to Jamaica aboard HMS Deptford. On arrival it is **just 5.1 seconds slow.** That should win the prize. It doesn't.

slides.title: It took a *king*
slides.body: The Board of Longitude keeps demanding more tests. In 1772 **King George III tests Harrison's H5 himself.** In 1773, aged 80, Harrison receives £8,750 from Parliament.

slides.title: Captain Cook called a copy of H4 *“our trusty friend.”*
slides.next: Cartier Santos: the watch made for a man who flew

caption:
Thousands of sailors died because nobody could fix a ship's position at sea. ⚓

In 1714 Britain offered a fortune to whoever solved the longitude problem. Everyone expected an astronomer. Instead, a self-taught carpenter spent decades building ever-better sea clocks, and his H4 changed navigation forever. Officially, the Longitude Prize was never awarded to anyone, though Harrison was eventually paid over £23,000.

Would you have backed the stars or the clock? 👇
